verdict.rationale: The verb daimonizomai (G1139) occurs 13 times, all in the Gospels, and is uniformly predicated of persons who are not disciples of Jesus. The grammar of these scenes is concretely spatial. Demons are said to enter into the man (eiserchomai eis auton, Luke 8:30) and to come out from the man (exerchomai apo or ek tou anthropou, Mark 1:26, Mark 5:8, Luke 8:33, Matthew 12:43, Acts 16:18). Jesus also says, never enter into him again (mēketi eiselthēs eis auton, Mark 9:25), and the cleared house can be re-inhabited and dwelt in (katoikei ekei, Matthew 12:45). The man can be described as ekhōn pneuma akatharton (Mark 1:23, Acts 19:13), having an unclean spirit, and in Acts 19:16 the spirit acts through the host with superhuman force. The lexical pattern across multiple authors and scenes pictures unbelieving or non-disciple persons as indwelt and controlled by spirits that can be expelled by command.

scripture.force: A man in the synagogue is described as anthrōpos en pneumati akathartō, a man in an unclean spirit. The preposition en plus the dative pictures the spirit as the medium or sphere in which the person now is, marking covert inhabitation rather than mere external proximity.

After Jesus rebukes the spirit, the spirit exēlthen ex autou, came out of him. The verb exerchomai with ek and the genitive person makes the host the spatial origin of departure, which presupposes the spirit was located inside the man.

A man with an unclean spirit, anthrōpos en pneumati akathartō, meets Jesus. The same en plus dative construction as Mark 1:23 locates the spirit as resident with and operative through the person, and the man is portrayed as an afflicted human, not as a disciple.

Jesus commands Exelthe to pneuma to akatharton ek tou anthrōpou, come out of the man. Ek plus the genitive of the host treats the man as the container from which the spirit must depart, which forecloses a merely external oppression reading.

The spirit answers Legiōn onoma moi, hoti polloi esmen, my name is Legion, for we are many. The first person speech through the man's mouth, and the self-naming, are lexical markers of inhabitation and operative control, not of an outside influence.

The healed man is named ton daimonizomenon, the one who had been demonized, now sitting clothed and sōphronounta, sound of mind. The participle marks his prior demonized state, and the restoration of soundness implies the demon had previously dominated his faculties.

Jesus commands the spirit exelthe ex autou kai mēketi eiselthēs eis auton, come out of him and never enter into him again. The paired exit and re-entry verbs with ek and eis plus the person make the man explicitly the spatial location of the spirit, and forbid future re-occupation.

Two daimonizomenoi, demonized men, meet Jesus from the tombs in the country of the Gadarenes. The participial form again marks an attested state of being demonized rather than a transient feeling, and the men are local sufferers, not followers of Jesus.

A blind and mute man is brought to Jesus as daimonizomenos, demonized, and the affliction is bound up with the demon so that healing the man casts out the demon. The man is an ordinary sufferer, not a disciple, and the demon is the cause of his disability.

Jesus speaks of casting out demons, ekballō ta daimonia, by the Spirit of God. The verb ekballō, to throw or drive out, presupposes the demon occupied the person, so that deliverance is an expulsion from within rather than a removal of an external pressure.

When the unclean spirit exelthē apo tou anthrōpou, goes out from the man, it wanders. The apo plus genitive of the person treats the man as the prior dwelling place. The same vocabulary as Mark 5:8 is used by another author, showing the pattern is not local to one writer.

The spirit returns with seven others and eiselthonta katoikei ekei, having entered, takes up residence there. Katoikeō is the standard verb for dwelling in a house. The image of the man as an inhabited dwelling is explicit and lexically forced.

Luke's parallel to Mark 5 adds the explicit grammar eisēlthen daimonia polla eis auton, many demons entered into him. Eiserchomai plus eis plus the accusative person is the strongest available Greek construction for an agent entering a container.

The demons exelthonta apo tou anthrōpou eisēlthon eis tous choirous, having come out from the man, entered into the pigs. The paired apo and eis construction in the same sentence shows transfer of indwelling from one host to another, which only coheres if indwelling is the operative concept.

Paul commands the spirit and it exelthen apo autēs, came out of her, at the same hour. The slave girl is a pagan diviner with a pneuma pythōna, and the apo plus genitive person construction mirrors the Gospel exorcism scenes. The vocabulary travels into Acts without change.

Jewish exorcists name Jesus over tous echontas ta pneumata ta ponēra, those having the evil spirits. The active participle of echō for the relationship between the host and the spirit is a stock lexical idiom for being inhabited, parallel to ekhōn daimonion in the Gospels.

The man ho anthrōpos en hō ēn to pneuma to ponēron, in whom the evil spirit was, overpowers seven exorcists. The relative clause en hō locates the spirit inside the man, and katakurieusas, having mastered them, shows the spirit acting through the unbelieving host with abnormal force.

complicating_texts.resolution: The bent woman is called a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound (edēsen) for eighteen years. The verb is deō, to bind, not daimonizomai, and the picture is external bondage rather than indwelling. So even a covenant member can be afflicted by Satan, but the specific lexical category of demonization with entering and exiting language is not applied here. The proposition about unbelievers being demonized is not threatened, because the verb under question is not used.

Luke writes eisēlthen Satanas eis Ioudan, Satan entered into Judas. This uses the exact eiserchomai eis auton construction that elsewhere marks demonic inhabitation. Judas is one of the Twelve in outward affiliation, yet the narrative consistently presents him as not a true disciple, son of perdition in John 17:12, devil in John 6:70. So this verse uses the lexical inhabitation construction of an outward follower whom the canon does not number among true believers. It refines rather than contradicts the proposition, since it confirms that the entering language is reserved for those outside true discipleship.

Peter says Satan eplērōsen, filled the heart of Ananias, a member of the early church. The verb is plēroō plus tēn kardian, fill the heart, not daimonizomai and not the eiserchomai eis auton container construction. The lexical category here is influence on the heart, not indwelling of the person. The narrative does not portray Ananias as demonized in the daimonizomai sense, so it does not extend that category to believers.

The slave girl has a pneuma pythōna, a python or divining spirit, and pythōn is a hapax legomenon in the New Testament, occurring only here. Its single occurrence prevents independent lexical triangulation of the term itself, but the case is anchored by the surrounding inhabitation grammar in verse 18 (exelthein apo autēs), which uses the standard exorcism vocabulary. So the scene still counts as an unbeliever indwelt by a spirit that is expelled by command.

variants.note: No variant units affecting the demonized condition were supplied or located. These passages fall outside the ECM-published scope of 3 John, so the manuscript picture is treated as ecm-shadow. The textual flags present in the SBLGNT apparatus, such as Gerasenes versus Gadarenes versus Gergesenes in Mark 5:1 and Matthew 8:28, are geographic and do not affect the lexical pattern of indwelling and expulsion.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reading only the verb daimonizomai yields the bare claim that a person is demonized, without specifying the degree of indwelling. A minimalist reading affirms that unbelievers in the Gospels are demonized but withholds judgment on the parenthetical phrase full inhabitation, since the verb itself does not encode a degree.

Attending to the syntax of indwelling, the en plus dative for the spirit's location in the man, the eis plus accusative for entering, the ek and apo plus genitive for exiting, the first person speech of the spirit through the man, and the superhuman strength in Acts 19:16, the narrative and grammar together describe inhabitation and operative control of unbelieving persons.

Reading daimonizomai as a wide term that covers severe demonic affliction including but not limited to indwelling, the proposition still holds: unbelievers in the Gospels and Acts are repeatedly placed under demonic affliction that requires expulsion. The cases of Mark 9:25 and Luke 8:30 nevertheless add concrete entering and exiting grammar that goes beyond mere oppression.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on the spatial prepositions en, eis, ek, and apo combined with the verbs eiserchomai, exerchomai, and ekballō, read across multiple Gospel and Acts scenes, with analogia scripturae confirming a consistent pattern across Mark, Matthew, Luke, and Acts.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Persons who are not disciples of Jesus are described in the Gospels and Acts as demonized, with spirits said to enter into them, dwell in them, speak through them, and be commanded out of them.
stem_audit.notes: The parenthetical full inhabitation in the stem preloads a degree term that the underlying verb daimonizomai does not lexically encode. The verb only states that a person is demonized. The degree of indwelling is inferred from the spatial prepositions and from the spirit speaking through the host and acting with its strength. The verdict was derived on the original stem, but the affirmation rests on the lexically demonstrable indwelling and operative control of unbelieving persons, not on a precise quantification of inhabitation.

lay_summary: The Greek verb behind these scenes is daimonizomai, usually rendered to be demonized. It occurs thirteen times in the New Testament, all in the Gospels, and it is always used of people who are not followers of Jesus. The reading is not just about a label on those people. The surrounding grammar is concretely spatial. Demons are said to enter into the person, using eis plus the accusative, as when Luke writes that many demons entered into the Gerasene man. They are said to come out from the person, using apo or ek plus the genitive, as when Jesus tells the spirit to come out of the man and never enter into him again. The man can be described as in an unclean spirit or as having an unclean spirit. The spirit can speak through the man's mouth in the first person, as when Legion answers Jesus, and the spirit can act through the man with more than human strength, as when the man in Acts overpowers seven exorcists. In Matthew the cleared person is even pictured as a house in which the spirit takes up residence. Across Mark, Matthew, Luke, and Acts the vocabulary is the same. The proposition has one honest limit. The verb itself does not carry a degree word. It says demonized, not the proportion. So the parenthetical full inhabitation in the question is an added description rather than something the word measures on its own. There is also a small group of edge texts where covenant members are pressured by Satan, such as the bent woman Satan had bound, or Ananias whose heart Satan filled. Those use different verbs, binding and filling, not the entering and exiting verbs used of the demonized. So the language reserved for indwelling continues to land on those outside true discipleship. What the words plainly show is that people who are not believers are pictured as inhabited and controlled by unclean spirits that can be commanded out.
